There is no such thing as true libertarianism. Heck there is no such thing as clear definition libertarianism. It can range from anarcho-capitiaism to libertarian socialism. Libertarians can't even agree on public education, roads, or fire protection, or the need of a national defence.

Would true libertarianism create extreme wealth and poverty?

Honestly depends on what you mean by libertarianism.

I don't think you create poverty. Poverty is the natural state of man. Wealth is from division of labor. Poverty today (in America) is people doing their own taxes, mending their own clothes, fixing their own cars because they have to. Wealthier people don't do general labor; they specialize and have others do everything else for them.

If you look at the extraordinarily poor in the third world, they also are generalists. They're hunter-gatherers in Sub-Saharian Africa, or they live in shacks they built themselves in Indian slums. They do everything for themselves.

But they're poor because they lack advancement. They don't become any poorer when their neighbors trade labor. They stayed the same, and other societies got richer.

Libertarianism won't make anyone more poor, but it'll make more rich people. It'll break down the trade barriers that prevent people from doing trade.

Difficult to say.

The most concerning part is the extreme poverty bit. (I have no objection if some other dude gets extremely rich.)

The question is whether our current welfare system reduces poverty, or increases it. Libertarians will assert that welfare tends to increase poverty rather than decrease it, by breaking the connection between work and income. If someone has a choice between working hard to take home $300 a week, or sitting around on their lazy ass for $250 a week, they'll almost always choose laziness. If they didn't have the option of laziness, they'd have to work. By working, they'd develop some skills, and eventually be able to do work that's worth more.

There's also cultural effects, what happens when you're a kid growing up in a neighbourhood where nobody works?

Anyway, libertarians tend to assume that by making people feel more responsible for their own selves, you can break the culture of slovenliness and dependence which possesses the lower end of society in most Western countries.

Would it work? Well, it's not like the current system is doing an admirable job of breaking poverty, that's for sure.
